title: Given a begin word, an end word, and a dictionary of equal-length words, return the length of the shortest transformation sequence from begin to end, where each step changes exactly one letter and every intermediate word is in the dictionary, or zero if none exists.
shortTitle: Word Ladder — BFS changing one letter at a time

s1_definition.profdef: Word Ladder models words as graph nodes with an edge between words differing by one letter, then runs breadth-first search from the begin word. Because BFS explores by distance, the first time it reaches the end word gives the shortest sequence length. Neighbors are generated by trying every single-letter change and keeping only dictionary words.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of transforming one account-status code into another by changing one character at a time, where every step must still be a valid code in the approved list. You explore all codes one change away, then all codes two changes away, and so on, in expanding waves. The first wave that reaches the target code tells you the fewest steps needed.
s1_definition.oneliner: Treat words as nodes with edges between one-letter-apart words and BFS from begin; the level at which end is first reached is the shortest ladder length.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Word Ladder models words as graph nodes with an edge between words differing by one letter, then runs breadth-first search from the begin word. Because BFS explores by distance, the first time it reaches the end word gives the shortest sequence length. Neighbors are generated by trying every single-letter change and keeping only dictionary words.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of transforming one account-status code into another by changing one character at a time, where every step must still be a valid code in the approved list. You explore all codes one change away, then all codes two changes away, and so on, in expanding waves. The first wave that reaches the target code tells you the fewest steps needed.

**One line to remember:** Treat words as nodes with edges between one-letter-apart words and BFS from begin; the level at which end is first reached is the shortest ladder length.

sections.s2_technical:
Put the dictionary into a hash set for constant-time membership checks, and start a BFS from the begin word with a distance of one. For example: `Set<String> dict = new HashSet<>(wordList);` and enqueue begin.

Process the queue level by level. For each word, generate every neighbor by changing each position to every other letter, and if a neighbor is in the dictionary and not yet visited, enqueue it and mark it visited. For example: for each index, try each letter a through z, forming a candidate and checking the set.

When a generated neighbor equals the end word, the current distance plus one is the answer, because BFS guarantees the first arrival is by a shortest path. For example: `if (candidate.equals(end)) return level + 1;`. If the queue empties without reaching end, return zero.

The time is the number of words times word length times the alphabet size, since each word spawns length times alphabet candidates, and the space is the dictionary and visited sets. A senior nuance is generating neighbors by single-letter substitution rather than comparing all word pairs, which avoids a quadratic adjacency build, and that bidirectional BFS from both ends can further cut the search space dramatically on large dictionaries.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, an account-status code must be migrated to a target code one character at a time, where every intermediate code must be a valid approved code. The system must find the fewest valid steps. This is exactly how Word Ladder works — shortest path over one-letter transformations.

Problem 2 — The approved-code list is large, so building all pairwise adjacencies would be wasteful. This is exactly why neighbors are generated by single-letter substitution and checked against a set.

The mini-project builds a `StatusMigrationPlanner` using BFS, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo migrating one code to another.

sections.s5_journey:
The input begins at hit, ends at cog, with valid codes hot, dot, dog, lot, log, cog.

Step 1: The dictionary is loaded into a set, cog is present, and BFS starts from hit at level one.

Step 2: Level one processes hit. Changing one letter yields hot, which is valid and unvisited, so hot is enqueued for level two.

Step 3: Level two processes hot, generating dot and lot, both valid, enqueued for level three.

Step 4: Level three processes dot and lot, generating dog and log, both valid, enqueued for level four.

Step 5: Level four processes dog and log, generating cog, which is valid, enqueued for level five.

Step 6: Level five processes cog, which equals the end word, so the answer is five, the length of the shortest ladder hit, hot, dot/lot, dog/log, cog.

```text
2026-10-26T22:25:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Account Status Code Migration
2026-10-26T22:25:00Z [INFO] Migrated 'hit' -> 'cog' in 5 steps
```

    L4: dog, log

sections.s6_takeaway:
Word Ladder asks for the shortest transformation from a begin word to an end word, changing one letter per step with every intermediate word in a dictionary. I model it as an implicit graph where words are nodes and an edge connects any two words differing by exactly one letter, then run breadth-first search from the begin word. Because BFS explores strictly by distance, the first time it reaches the end word gives the shortest sequence length.

I load the dictionary into a hash set for constant-time membership checks and process the queue level by level, treating each level as one transformation step. For each word I generate neighbors by changing each position to every other letter, keeping only candidates that are in the dictionary and not yet visited, enqueueing those for the next level. When a candidate equals the end word, the current level plus one is the answer; if the queue empties first, no path exists and I return zero.

The efficiency point interviewers want is generating neighbors by single-letter substitution rather than comparing all pairs of words, which avoids an expensive quadratic adjacency build, and I mention bidirectional BFS from both ends as a way to shrink the search space dramatically on large dictionaries. The cost is the number of words times word length times alphabet size.

In my project at National Bank of India, an account-status code sometimes had to migrate to a target code one character at a time, with every intermediate code required to be an approved valid code. Finding the fewest valid steps was this exact problem, and BFS over single-letter substitutions checked against the approved-code set gave the shortest migration path without ever building the full adjacency between all codes.
